title: Annotate Command Term IB: What It Means
summary: Annotate command term IB guidance with clear definitions, worked Biology, Geography and Economics examples, and practical exam-answering advice.
body_markdown:
A student sees **annotate** in an IB exam question and thinks the task looks easy. There is already a diagram. Surely a few labels will do.


That assumption often produces an incomplete answer. The **annotate command term IB** definition is precise: **add brief notes to a diagram or graph** . Those notes must go beyond merely naming visible features. They should attach concise, relevant information to specific parts of the visual.


Imagine a hypothetical IB student named Maya improving one Biology response across three drafts. Her first draft labels a structure. Her second adds a fact. Her third connects each short note to the correct visual feature. The improvement is small on the page, but important in the thinking: she has moved from identifying to annotating.


The practical rule is simple: **point to the relevant feature, name it where necessary, and add a short note that communicates knowledge about it** .


### The annotate command term IB checklist


Before moving on from an annotation question, check that you have:


- Written directly on or beside the diagram or graph
- Connected each note to a precise feature with an arrow or clear placement
- Added information rather than only naming the feature
- Used short, subject-specific phrases
- Addressed the focus of the question
- Kept every note legible and unambiguous
- Avoided turning annotations into detached paragraphs


If the visual could be removed and your answer would still look almost the same, you may not be annotating. A strong response depends on the relationship between the note and the feature it identifies.


For broader context, RevisionDojo's[complete IB exam command terms guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-exam-command-terms-list) shows how the instruction word changes the expected shape of an answer.


A student has covered a large plant with notes while a teacher suggests that the plant wants fewer annotations.


### How one annotation improves across drafts


Suppose Maya receives a simplified diagram of a cell membrane and is asked to annotate it to show how its structure supports transport.


### Draft one: a label without a note


> Channel protein


This identifies a structure. It does not yet explain anything about that structure, so it is closer to **label** than **annotate** .


### Draft two: a relevant but loose fact


> Channel protein allows ions through.


The scientific information is better, but Maya writes it beneath the diagram without indicating which membrane component it describes. A knowledgeable examiner might infer the connection, but the visual relationship is unclear.


### Draft three: a true annotation


Maya draws an arrow to the transmembrane protein and writes:


> Channel protein: hydrophilic passage permits specific ions to cross the membrane.


Now the note is brief, scientifically relevant and attached to the correct feature. If the question asks for several annotations, Maya repeats this pattern across distinct parts of the diagram rather than writing one general explanation.


Students can practise this difference through the[IB Biology Questionbank](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-biology-new/questionbank) . The accompanying[IB Biology command terms examples](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-biology-command-terms-explained) are also useful when deciding how much depth each instruction requires.


### How annotate differs from similar IB command terms


Several **IB command terms** appear similar because they can all involve visual material. Their answer shapes are not identical.


Command term What the response should do


Label Add a name or identifier to a feature


Annotate Add brief informative notes to specific features of a diagram or graph


Identify Provide the required name, feature or answer


Describe Give a detailed account of what can be observed or how something appears


Explain Give reasons, causes or mechanisms that make the outcome understandable


Consider a graph showing unemployment rising from 5% to 8%.


A **label** might name the vertical axis as “Unemployment rate (%)”. An **annotation** could point to the rising section and state, “Unemployment increases by 3 percentage points during this period.” A **description** would give a connected account of the pattern. An **explanation** would address why the increase occurred, using relevant economic reasoning or contextual evidence.


This distinction protects your time. An annotation normally needs more than a label but less continuous prose than an extended explanation. RevisionDojo's guide to[using IB command terms effectively](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-use-ib-command-terms-effectively-in-exam-responses) can help you develop a repeatable response shape for each verb.


### How to annotate IB visuals across subjects


The core definition remains stable, but useful annotations depend on the subject and the exact question. A Biology diagram rewards biological information. A Geography map needs spatially precise observations. An Economics diagram requires accurate relationships between curves, axes and outcomes.


### Biology: attach function to structure


Imagine a diagram of a chloroplast. A weak response labels a stack as “granum.” A stronger annotation points to it and adds:


> Granum: stacked thylakoids provide membranes containing photosynthetic pigments.


The note does not attempt to reproduce an entire textbook explanation. It contributes one relevant piece of knowledge tied to the visible structure.


A useful Biology formula is:


> **feature + relevant property, function or process**


For more subject-specific practice, students can review RevisionDojo's guide to[understanding IB Biology command terms](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-understand-ib-biology-command-terms-for-exam-success) .


### Geography: make the spatial link precise


Suppose a map shows settlements concentrated beside a river. Maya initially writes, “Many settlements here.” The word “here” is vague, and no symbol or arrow establishes its location.


She improves it to:


> Arrow to riverside cluster: dense linear settlement follows the river valley.


A second note might point to an upland area:


> Sparse settlement on higher ground away from the main transport corridor.


Good geographical annotations combine location with a concise observation. If the question asks for evidence from a map, graph or image, generic subject knowledge cannot replace what the source actually shows. The[IB Geography Questionbank](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-geography/questionbank) gives students a place to practise selecting visual evidence under realistic constraints.

They do not replace analysis if the question separately asks students to explain causes or evaluate policy. ### How annotations are rewarded


There is no universal rule stating that every annotation earns one mark. Marks depend on the subject, question and markscheme. What remains consistent is that examiners can only credit relevant knowledge that is communicated clearly enough to satisfy the task.


A successful annotation usually contains three elements:


- **Correct placement:** the arrow or note clearly targets the intended feature
- **Accurate content:** the information is valid for the subject and visual
- **Relevant detail:** the note answers the question rather than adding a memorized fact


Several vague comments pointing toward the same feature may add less value than two precise, distinct notes. Repetition does not create additional understanding. Neither does decorative complexity. Your goal is to make each marking point easy to find.


Also read the wording around the command term. “Annotate the graph to show two impacts” creates a clear numerical requirement. “Draw and annotate” requires both an appropriate visual and attached notes. If another command term follows, such as “explain,” the annotations alone may not complete the whole task.


### A practical annotation routine for exam day


Maya's final improvement is not a longer answer. It is a more controlled process:


1. Circle the command term mentally or on the paper.
2. Identify how many notes the wording or marks appear to require.
3. Find the exact features that answer the question.
4. Draw short, unambiguous arrows where needed.
5. Write one useful fact beside each feature.
6. Check that the notes are distinct, accurate and readable.

Maya's three drafts reveal the deeper lesson. IB exams do not reward the amount of ink on the page. They reward evidence that matches the instruction. When you see **annotate** , do not write everything you know. Find the right feature, attach the right note and make the connection unmistakable.
